text: Yes. Until about 10,000 years ago, the Americas were home to giant ground sloths. The biggest, Megatherium of South America and its close cousin Eremotherium, were up to about 6 m long and weighed around 4 tonnes, about as much as an elephant.

They were plant-eaters with huge curved claws. Instead of hanging in trees, they lived on the ground. They could rear up on their back legs and tail to tear down branches from tall trees. Today's [[@power-sloth|small tree sloths]] are their distant relatives.

st.prompt: Giant ground sloths had huge curved claws on their hands. How did they walk?

st.reveal: Their claws were too big to walk on flat-handed. Like anteaters today, they turned their hands to walk on the knuckles and the outer edges of their feet. That protected the claws for pulling branches and digging.

sec.t:
In 1788, a huge skeleton was dug up near the river Luján in [[@argentina|Argentina]], then ruled by Spain. It was shipped to Madrid and put together for the king's natural history collection. In 1796, the French scientist Georges Cuvier studied drawings of it and named it Megatherium, "great beast".

Cuvier saw that it was related to living sloths and anteaters, yet nothing like it was alive anywhere. This helped convince him that some animals had gone [[extinct|extinct]], an idea many people found hard to accept then.

Giant sloths had peg-like teeth with no hard [[enamel|enamel]], which kept growing all their lives, good for grinding tough leaves. Their claws were so big that they could not walk flat-handed. Instead they walked on their knuckles and on the outer edges of their feet.

Their bones show strong hips and a thick tail, which formed a tripod when they stood up. Some may also have dug burrows. In Brazil and Argentina, large [[@tunnels|tunnels]] in the rock, wide enough for a person to walk through, have scratch marks thought to be from giant sloths or giant armadillo relatives.

Some of the best clues come from a smaller [[species|species]], the Shasta ground sloth. In dry [[@caves-form|caves]] in Nevada and [[@grand-canyon-state|Arizona]], including Rampart Cave near the [[@grand-canyon|Grand Canyon]], its dung piled up for thousands of years. The desert air dried it out.

Scientists picked through the dung and found what the sloths ate: desert globemallow, saltbush and other plants that still grow nearby. In 1976, a fire started in Rampart Cave and smouldered for months, burning much of the dung.

Giant ground sloths vanished from the mainland around 10,000 years ago, along with [[@mammoths|mammoths]], [[@sabre-tooth|sabre-toothed cats]] and many other big animals of the [[@ice-ages|ice ages]]. The [[climate|climate]] was changing, and [[@lost-moa|humans had recently arrived]]. Some sloth bones carry cut marks from human tools.

On a few Caribbean islands, which people reached much later, smaller ground sloths survived for thousands of years longer. Their story is one clue that people played a big part in the giants' disappearance. Today's tree sloths, which weigh only a few kilograms, are all that is left of the family.

text: A desert is any place that gets very little rain or snow. Whether it ends up sandy or rocky depends mostly on two things: what kind of rock is around, and what the wind does.

In most deserts, wind blows away the loose [[@sand-where|sand]] and dust, leaving behind rock, gravel and pebbles too heavy to move. The sand piles up somewhere else, usually in low basins where the wind slows down. Those places become seas of [[@earth-weird-moving-dunes|dunes]]. So rocky deserts and sandy deserts are often two halves of the same story.

st.reveal: According to the US Geological Survey, sand covers only about 20% of the world's deserts. Much of the rest is bare rock, gravel plains, dry lake beds and mountains.

The sand drifts away and piles up at the far edge, while the pebbles stay behind, like a rocky desert floor.
myth: All deserts are hot and sandy.
A desert is defined by how little rain or snow it gets, not by heat or sand. The Gobi in Mongolia has freezing winters, and Antarctica, the largest desert on Earth, is covered in ice.
facts: a place that gets very little rain or snow, usually under 250 mm a year

sec.t:
With few plants to hold the ground together, desert wind can move a lot of material. It works like a sieve. Fine dust is lifted high and can be carried across oceans. Dust from the Sahara regularly reaches the Caribbean and even the [[@brazil-amazon|Amazon rainforest]].

Sand grains are heavier. They bounce along close to the ground, rarely rising higher than your waist. Pebbles and stones are too heavy for the wind to shift at all. Over thousands of years, the wind strips away the small grains and leaves a tightly packed layer of pebbles on the surface. [[geologist|Geologists]] call this desert pavement. It can look as if someone laid it out by hand.

Most desert sand is made of quartz, a hard mineral that survives after softer [[@rocks-types|rocks]] have crumbled. Desert rocks break down as they heat up by day and cool at night, and in sudden rainstorms that rush through [[@valleys|dry valleys]].

Rivers, often from long ago, also carry sand into deserts. Much of the sand in the [[@thar-formed|Thar Desert]] of Rajasthan is thought to have come from rivers and the dry beds of old streams. Strong summer winds from the southwest then shaped it into dunes.

Most of the world's desert land is rocky. There are wide plains of gravel, bare rock and mountains, and dry lake beds that shine white with salt. [[@mystery-sailing-stones|Death Valley]] in California is mostly rock, [[@earth-salt-flats|salt flats]] and stony fans spreading out from canyons. It has dunes too, but they cover only a small part of the park.

The [[@ladakh|Ladakh]] region of India is a high, cold desert, with bare mountains and rocky valleys. It gets so little rain because the Himalaya blocks [[@monsoon|the monsoon]] clouds before they arrive.

Because a desert is about dryness, not heat, the largest desert on Earth is [[@antarctica|Antarctica]]. Very little snow falls there each year, but because it hardly ever melts, it has built up into [[@what-if-ice-melted|ice sheets kilometres thick]]. The Gobi Desert in [[@mongolia|Mongolia]] and China is rocky and gravelly, with scorching summers and bitterly cold winters.

Deserts are not empty. Plants grow wide, shallow roots to catch rare rain, or deep ones to reach water underground. Animals hide from the heat by day. People have lived in deserts for thousands of years, from the Rajasthani villages of the Thar to the [[@navajo-nation|Navajo Nation]] in the American Southwest. [[@desert-life|Life in the desert]] depends on knowing exactly where water can be found.

text: Fog is a cloud that sits on the ground. It forms when air near the surface cools until its water vapour turns into billions of tiny droplets. Weather experts call it fog when it cuts visibility to less than 1 km. It is just water, and it disappears once the air warms up.

Smog is polluted air. The word was made by joining "smoke" and "fog" over a hundred years ago, when coal smoke mixed with fog in cities like London. Today, it also means the brownish haze made when sunlight cooks car exhaust, as in [[@los-angeles|Los Angeles]].
In north India in winter, you often get both: natural fog and thick pollution, trapped together near the ground.

st.prompt: On a clear, calm winter night, why is fog more likely to form by morning than on a cloudy night?

options.t: Heat escapes into space, so the ground and air near it cool quickly
Stars give off cold light that chills the air
Clouds usually soak up fog before it forms

st.reveal: Clouds act like a blanket, sending heat back down. Without them, the ground loses heat fast. The air touching it cools until its water vapour condenses into tiny droplets, and you wake up to fog.

sec.t:
Air always holds some invisible water vapour. Cold air can hold less than warm air. When moist air cools enough, the extra vapour [[condensation|condenses]] onto specks of dust, salt or soot, making droplets far too small to fall as rain.

On clear, still winter nights, the ground loses heat quickly to the sky, chilling the air just above it. By dawn, fields and roads can disappear in white. This happens often across the plains of [[@punjab|Punjab]], Haryana, Uttar Pradesh and Bihar, delaying trains and flights.

Another kind forms when warm, damp air drifts over cold water. Summer fog rolls in through the Golden Gate in [[@san-francisco|San Francisco]] this way, as moist ocean air passes over a cold current along the coast.

sec.h: The smog that changed a city

sec.t:
Los Angeles had a different kind of smog. By the 1940s, the city was often covered in a brown haze that stung people's eyes, even on sunny days without fog. In the 1950s, a chemist named Arie Haagen-Smit showed what was happening. Sunlight was acting on gases from car exhaust, making new pollutants. One of them is [[ozone|ozone]] close to the ground.

High up, in the [[@ozone-layer|ozone layer]], ozone protects us from the Sun's [[ultraviolet|ultraviolet]] rays. Down where we breathe, it irritates the lungs. Cleaner cars and stricter rules have made Los Angeles air much better than it was, though it still has bad days.

[[@delhi|Delhi]] often gets the worst of both worlds. In winter, cold air sits under a layer of warmer air, like a lid on a pot. This is called a temperature inversion. Smoke from vehicles, factories, building dust and crop burning in nearby states gets trapped under that lid. Add natural fog, and the city can disappear into grey for days.

The Air Quality Index, shown on apps and news screens, tells people how bad the air is. On very poor days, schools sometimes close and doctors advise children to play indoors. If the air makes you cough or your chest feel tight, tell an adult. Cities from Delhi to Beijing are trying to cut [[@air-pollution|air pollution]] with cleaner fuels, electric buses and limits on burning.

text: For human ears, yes. Sound is a wave of squashing and stretching that travels through stuff, like air, water or rock. Space is nearly a [[vacuum|vacuum]], almost empty of anything to squash. So a sound has nothing to travel through. If two astronauts on a spacewalk shouted at each other without radios, they would hear nothing.

But space isn't quite empty everywhere. Giant clouds of thin gas fill [[galaxy|galaxies]] and galaxy clusters, and planets like Mars have air. In those places, sound-like waves do travel, sometimes in very strange ways.

st.prompt: Two astronauts float in space without radios, helmets touching. Can they hear each other talk?

st.reveal: Sound needs something to travel through. Empty space has almost nothing, but two touching helmets are solid. The sound of a voice can shake one helmet, then the other, and reach the ears faintly.

sec.t:
On the Moon, there's no air at all. When Apollo astronauts dropped tools, the tools hit the ground silently. The astronauts could only talk to each other by radio, which uses light-like waves that need nothing to travel through.

Their own voices still worked inside the spacesuit, because the suit was full of air. And if a hammer hit the ground right beside an astronaut's boot, the shake could travel up through the suit and be felt more than heard. The way [[@sound-travel|sound travels]] through solids explains that.

Mars has air, thin but real, about one percent as thick as Earth's. In 2021, NASA's Perseverance [[rover|rover]] landed with microphones and recorded the first sounds from the surface: wind, the crack of its laser zapping rocks, and the whirr of the Ingenuity helicopter.

Scientists found that sound on Mars travels at about 240 m/s, slower than on Earth. Even stranger, high-pitched sounds travel a little faster than low ones. Mars air is mostly [[carbon-dioxide|carbon dioxide]], which behaves oddly with sound at that low pressure. Sounds also fade faster, so you would need to stand close to hear a friend. The story of [[@mars-rovers|the Mars rovers]] has more of their discoveries.

Inside the International Space Station, it is far from quiet. Fans and pumps run day and night to move air around. Without fans, the carbon dioxide astronauts breathe out would gather round their faces, because warm air doesn't rise in weightlessness. Astronauts often wear earplugs to sleep.

Spacecraft can also pick up waves in thin charged gas, called [[plasma|plasma]], around planets. Scientists turn these readings into sound so people can hear them. Recordings from the Voyager probes, sent out in 1977, include eerie whistles from Jupiter's magnetic field.

Space films usually ignore all this and add roaring engines and booming explosions. That isn't the science, it's the storytelling, a habit that took hold when the first [[@star-wars-effect|Star Wars]] film filled the screen with roaring spaceships.

text: A tidal bore is a wave that travels up a river, against the flow, when the tide comes in. Most river mouths just fill up gently as the sea rises. But in a few places, the incoming tide is so strong, and the river mouth so shallow and narrow, that the seawater piles up into a wall and charges upstream.

From the bank, it looks as if the river suddenly reverses. A rumble comes first, then a wave, from a small ripple to several metres high, rolls past. Behind it, the river is higher, choppy and flowing the wrong way.

st.reveal: Bores form where big tides rush into a shallow estuary that narrows quickly. The water piles up as the funnel squeezes it, forming a step-like wave that pushes upstream.

sec.t:
A bore needs two things. First, a big [[@tides|tide]]. Tides are caused by the pull of the Moon and Sun, and in some places the difference between high and low tide is many metres.

Second, it needs a river mouth shaped like a funnel: wide and shallow at the sea, narrowing quickly inland. As the tide rushes in, the funnel squeezes it, and the water can't spread out fast enough. It rears up into a step-shaped wave. Bores are biggest around full moon and new moon, when the Sun and Moon pull together, giving the strongest "spring" tides. Only a small number of rivers in the world have strong bores.

Bores are a surfer's dream: a wave that keeps going for kilometres. The pororoca on the Amazon, in Brazil, can travel far inland. Its name comes from a local language word for "great roar". Surfers hold competitions on it.

In England, surfers ride the Severn bore, which can reach about 2 m. Some rides have lasted more than half an hour. In Alaska, the bore in Turnagain Arm, near Anchorage, also draws surfers wearing thick wetsuits against the cold. It's one of the few places where [[@sport-surfing|surfing]] means riding a river.

India has bores too. On the Hooghly River near [[@kolkata|Kolkata]], the bore is called the "baan". In the days of sailing ships, it could tip over small boats, and sailors timed their trips carefully. Today, the baan is smaller, partly because the river has changed.

The Gulf of Khambhat in Gujarat has some of the biggest tides in India, with a range of up to about 10 m. Bores travel up rivers that flow into it, such as the Narmada and Mahi.

Bores churn up mud and stir food from the riverbed. Birds gather to feed on fish and shrimps tumbling in the foam. Fish that live in [[estuary|estuaries]] have adapted to the sudden change from fresh to salty water.

Across the Atlantic, the Bay of Fundy in Canada has the world's highest tides, up to about 16 m between high and low water. Small bores run up rivers there too. The [[rhythm|rhythm]] of all these bores, like every tide, is set by the Moon, whose pull has shaped coasts for billions of years and may even have helped [[@moon-tides-life|life on Earth]] begin.

text: Big cats and house cats belong to the same family, the Felidae. They share an ancestor that lived millions of years ago, so they are built in much the same way. All cats walk on their toes, have sharp curved claws, eyes that see well in dim light and teeth made for slicing meat.

They also behave alike. A tiger in Ranthambore and a cat on a sofa in Chennai both stalk, pounce, groom their fur with a rough tongue and nap for long parts of the day. The biggest differences are size, how they make sounds and how they live with people. A big male tiger can weigh about fifty times as much as a house cat.

sec.t:
Every cat is a meat eater. Their tongues are covered in tiny backward-pointing hooks that scrape meat off bones and comb their fur. Their back teeth work like scissors, not grinders, so they slice food rather than chew it.

Most cats can pull their claws in to keep them sharp. That is why a house cat scratches a sofa, and a [[@tiger-stripes|tiger]] scrapes a tree trunk. Both are sharpening claws and leaving scent from [[gland|glands]] in their paws. The cheetah is the odd one out. Its claws stay partly out, like a sprinter's spiked shoes.

Most cats hunt alone, by stalking and ambush. They creep up low, freeze, then burst forward. A house cat watching a sparrow and a leopard watching a deer go through almost the same routine. Even the tail twitch and the little wiggle of the back legs before the pounce are the same. Both cats are checking their grip and balance before they spring.

Lions are the exception. They live in groups called prides, and the females often hunt together. India's [[@lions-gir|Asiatic lions]] in Gir live in smaller groups than African lions, but they still share food and raise cubs together.

India has about 15 kinds of wild cat, more than any other country. The big ones are the tiger, Asiatic lion, leopard, snow leopard and clouded leopard. The small ones include the jungle cat, fishing cat, leopard cat, caracal and desert cat.

The rusty-spotted cat, found in India and Sri Lanka, is among the smallest cats in the world, weighing about a kilogram. In 2022 India counted about 3,700 tigers, around three-quarters of all wild tigers. Cheetahs died out in India by the 1950s, and in 2022 the country began bringing them in from Africa to [[@cheetah-return|Kuno National Park]].

sec.h: How house cats came to live with us
sec.t:
House cats come from the African wildcat. About 10,000 years ago, when people in the Middle East began storing grain, mice moved in, and wildcats followed the mice. People seem to have welcomed them.

A grave in Cyprus, about 9,500 years old, holds a person buried with a cat. Later, the [[@ancient-egypt|ancient Egyptians]] kept cats in homes and temples. Today there are hundreds of millions of house cats. Under the fur, each one is still a small hunter.

text: The small striped squirrels you see across India are palm squirrels. Their stripes are part of their fur pattern, passed down from parents to babies through their [[@genes-family|genes]], just like a tiger's stripes or a zebra's.
Scientists think the stripes help squirrels blend in. Light and dark lines break up the outline of the body, so a squirrel on a branch dappled with sunlight is harder for a hawk or a cat to spot.
But many Indian children first hear a different answer, from a story. It has nothing to do with [[gene|genes]], and a lot to do with kindness.

sec.h: The story of the helpful squirrel
sec.t:
In the [[@ramayana|Ramayana]], Rama's army of monkeys and bears builds a bridge across the sea to Lanka, to rescue Sita. In one much-loved retelling, a little squirrel wants to help too.

It rolls in the sand on the beach, runs onto the bridge and shakes the sand off between the stones. It does this again and again. Some of the monkeys laugh at such a tiny helper.

Rama picks up the squirrel and gently strokes its back with three fingers. The marks of his fingers become its stripes. The story is told to show that even the smallest effort matters. It isn't in every version of the Ramayana, but it is told in homes across India.

There are two common kinds. The three-striped palm squirrel lives mostly in southern India and Sri Lanka. The five-striped palm squirrel is more common in the north, from Gujarat to Bengal, and also in Nepal and Pakistan.

Both kinds have three bold pale stripes down the back. The five-striped squirrel has two extra fainter stripes along its sides. Look closely at the one on your wall or mango tree and count.

Palm squirrels are busy in the daytime. They eat seeds, fruit, flowers and insects, and they often live close to people. Their high, chattering call, often with a flick of the tail, warns others of a cat or a [[@crow-smart|crow]].

India also has squirrels that look nothing like the little striped ones. The Indian giant squirrel lives in forests in the [[@western-ghats|Western Ghats]] and central India. Its fur is a mix of maroon, brown and cream, and from nose to tail tip it can be about a metre long, as long as a cricket bat.

It is the state animal of Maharashtra, where it is called shekru. It rarely comes to the ground and can leap about 6 m between trees.

India has flying squirrels too. They don't really fly. They stretch out folds of skin between their legs and glide from tree to tree at night.

{{story:tiger-stripes}}

In much of the USA, the squirrel everyone knows is the eastern grey squirrel. It has no stripes. Each autumn it buries thousands of acorns and nuts, one at a time, in shallow holes.

Scientists once thought squirrels just sniffed around for nuts in winter. Experiments show they remember many of their hiding places and use smell to find the exact spot. Some squirrels even pretend to bury a nut when another animal is watching, then hide it somewhere else.

Still, some buried nuts are never dug up. They sprout into seedlings, and a few grow into oak and walnut trees. In this way squirrels help forests spread, which makes them some of the busiest tree planters around.

Unlike chipmunks and ground squirrels, tree squirrels don't hibernate. On cold days they curl up in a leafy nest called a drey and wait for better weather.

text: A barcode is a number written in stripes. Each digit is turned into a pattern of black bars and white gaps of different widths.

[[@scanners|A scanner]] shines red light across the stripes. White gaps bounce the light back, and black bars soak it up. A [[sensor|sensor]] records the flickering pattern of bright and dark, and a tiny computer turns it back into digits. Then the shop's computer looks up that number to find the product's name and price.

sec.t:
In the late 1940s, an American student named Joseph Woodland was trying to find a way for grocery shops to record what they sold. Sitting on a beach in Miami, he drew the dots and dashes of [[@codes-morse|Morse code]] in the sand with his fingers. Then he pulled them downwards into long thin and thick lines.

That was the idea. Woodland and his friend Bernard Silver patented a barcode in 1952. One of their designs was a bullseye of circles, which could be read from any direction. Scanners good enough to read it cheaply didn't exist yet, so the idea waited more than 20 years.

sec.h: The last digit checks the others
sec.t:
The 13th digit is not part of the product number. It's a *check digit*, worked out from the other twelve with a simple sum. If a scanner misreads one bar, the sum no longer matches and the scanner refuses to beep. The cashier tries again.

You can do this sum yourself. Books use it too: their barcode is their ISBN number, which starts with 978. Take the example number 978030640615. The sum gives 7, and that is exactly the final digit printed on the book.

Older scanners used a red [[@lasers|laser]] that swept across the stripes with a spinning mirror. Many newer ones are tiny [[@cameras-how|cameras]] that photograph the whole code at once.

Ordinary barcodes can only be read in one direction and hold a short number. [[@qr-codes|QR codes]], invented in Japan in 1994, pack information into a square grid of dots, so they can hold a whole web address. That's the kind you scan to pay at an Indian tea stall with UPI. Inside the computer, both kinds end up as [[@binary-code|binary]], long strings of 0s and 1s.

Barcodes now track parcels, airline bags, library books, hospital wristbands and medicine packets. Couriers scan a single box many times between a warehouse and your door, so they always know where it is. A painted letter on a [[@lunchbox-dabbawala|dabbawala]]'s lunchbox and a striped label on a parcel are doing the same job: making a long address short enough to read at a glance.

text: In India, most cars and trucks carry a FASTag, a small sticker on the inside of the windscreen. Hidden inside is a tiny chip and a thin metal antenna. As a vehicle rolls into a toll lane, a reader mounted above the road sends out radio waves.

Those waves power the chip for a moment, and it sends back a unique number. A computer matches that number to a bank account or wallet, takes the toll, and tells the barrier to lift. A text message pings the owner's phone, showing the amount and the name of the toll plaza. The whole exchange takes a fraction of a second. This technology is called RFID, short for radio frequency identification.

sec.t:
For decades, Indian highway tolls meant stopping at a booth, finding change and waiting for a paper receipt. Queues on busy days could stretch for kilometres. FASTag was tested on the Mumbai–Ahmedabad highway in 2014 and spread across the country over the next few years.

In February 2021 it became compulsory for vehicles on national highways. Drivers without a tag had to pay double in cash. Within months, nearly all toll payments on national highways were electronic. Stopping, paying and waiting for change could take minutes at a busy plaza. With a working tag, most cars now roll through in well under a minute, and drivers burn less fuel idling in queues. The tag is linked to a bank account, and payments can be topped up through apps that use [[@upi-payments|UPI]].

In August 2025, the government launched a FASTag annual pass for private cars. For ₹3,000, a driver gets up to 200 toll crossings on national highways in a year. Lakhs of drivers signed up in the first few days, and more than 77 lakh passes had been issued by June 2026. The price rose to ₹3,075 in April 2026.

There are rules too. Since 2024, each vehicle can have only one working FASTag, to stop people sharing tags between cars. Tags can stop working if a windscreen has a tinted film with metal in it, because metal blocks the radio signal. In that case drivers can fix the tag to the headlamp area instead.

sec.h: Tolls in America and the future
sec.t:
The USA started using electronic toll tags earlier. The Dallas North Tollway in Texas introduced its TollTag in 1989, and E-ZPass began in New York in 1993. E-ZPass now works across many states. Some American roads have no booths at all. Overhead gantries read tags, and cameras photograph number plates and post a bill to cars without one.

India is testing similar barrier-free lanes, with cameras that read number plates at speed. It is also exploring tolls worked out by satellite, using [[@gps-how|GPS]]-style tracking to charge drivers for the exact distance they travel. If that happens, the toll booth itself may slowly disappear from India's highways, as it already has from some roads in the USA.

text: The best paper plane depends on what you want. For distance, fold a slim, pointy dart with small, stiff wings and throw it hard and slightly upwards. For time in the air, fold a glider with wide wings and launch it gently. In both cases, three things matter most: the weight should sit towards the nose, the two sides must match exactly, and every fold should be sharp.
Small tweaks make a big difference. Bending the back edges of the wings by a millimetre or two can turn a plane that dives into one that glides across the room.

Bend the back edges of the wings sharply up

st.reveal: Back edges bent up push the tail down and the nose up, so the plane climbs too steeply and stalls. Flattening them, or bending them down a touch, lets the nose drop a little so the plane glides smoothly.

sec.h: Four forces on a sheet of paper
sec.t:
A paper plane obeys the same rules as a jumbo jet. Your arm gives it thrust. [[gravity|Gravity]] pulls it down. Air rushing over the wings gives lift, and air pushing against it causes drag, which slows it down.

A real plane keeps its engines running. A paper plane gets only one push, so from the moment it leaves your hand it is gliding, trading height and speed for distance. The longer it can keep that trade going, the better it flies. That is also how [[@gliders|engineless gliders]] soar.

The back edges of the wings act like the moving flaps on a real plane. Bend both up slightly and the tail is pushed down, so the nose rises. Bend both down and the nose dips. Bend one up and one down and the plane rolls and turns.

[[symmetry|Symmetry]] matters too. If one wing is even slightly bigger or more bent, the plane will curve to one side. Champion folders check their planes from the front, by eye, before every throw, and fold on a hard table with a thumbnail pressed along each crease.

In December 2025, a six-person team of Chinese students, average age about 17, threw an A4 paper plane 98.43 m in a big exhibition hall in Shanghai. Guinness World Records confirmed it, beating a record of about 88 m set in 2022. Records like this are flown indoors, where no wind can help. How Guinness checks such claims is explained in [[@world-records|world records]].

The record for time in the air was long held by Takuo Toda of Japan, whose glider stayed up 29.2 seconds in 2010. In February 2026, the same Chinese team beat it with a flight of 31.2 seconds, which Guinness World Records later confirmed. For time records, the plane is thrown almost straight up, as high as possible, then left to drift down in slow circles.

Distance planes are narrow and heavy for their size. They cut through the air with little drag and keep their speed. Throwers launch them hard, upwards at a steep angle, like a cricketer hurling the ball in from the boundary.

Time planes have big, broad wings and are light for their size, so they float like a falling leaf. Paper type matters too: thin, stiff paper folds crisply and holds its shape. And the science doesn't stop at the classroom window. The same balance and flap tricks keep real [[@airplanes-fly|aeroplanes]] steady in the sky.

text: Phulkari, meaning "flower work", is a kind of [[embroidery|embroidery]] from [[@punjab|Punjab]]. Women traditionally stitched it onto shawls and head-coverings called *odhnis*, using shiny silk thread on coarse, hand-spun cotton.

The patterns are mostly geometric: diamonds, triangles, stripes and stars. Some phulkaris have flowers scattered across the cloth. In the most splendid kind, called a *bagh*, which means garden, the stitches cover the cloth so completely that you can hardly see the fabric underneath. Phulkari belongs to the whole Punjab region, which today is split between [[@pakistan-history|India and Pakistan]].

st.reveal: Most phulkari was done without any drawing. Women counted the threads of the coarse cotton and built up shapes stitch by stitch, keeping the whole pattern in their heads.

Golden yellow on deep red is the best-known look, but old phulkaris also use white, green, pink, blue and more. Some styles, like sainchi, show whole scenes of village life, animals and people.

sec.t:
Phulkari uses a simple stitch called a darn stitch: long straight stitches on top, with tiny picks of the needle underneath. The embroiderer works from the back of the cloth. She counts the threads of the cotton to place each stitch, usually without drawing anything first.

The silk thread, called *pat*, was soft and untwisted, so it spread out and caught the light. By changing the direction of the stitches, a woman could make one shape shine and the next look darker, even with the same colour. This play of light gives a bagh its shimmer, like sunlight on a field of mustard.

The pattern grows outward from the middle. Often the embroiderer starts in the centre of the cloth and works toward the edges, repeating the same shapes again and again. Many baghs have near-perfect [[@symmetry|symmetry]]. Some include one small [[motif|motif]] in a different colour, which is often said to ward off the evil eye.

In 1947, [[@partition|Partition]] divided Punjab between India and Pakistan. Millions of families had to leave their homes. Some carried phulkaris with them as one of the few things they could save, and these pieces became precious links to lost villages.

The upheaval also broke the old chain of learning. With families scattered and machine-made cloth everywhere, fewer women made a bagh by hand. Many old pieces are now in museums such as the Victoria and Albert Museum in London. Collectors and families still treasure the ones that survived, and some have been passed down through four or five generations.

Phulkari never vanished. Today women in Patiala, [[@amritsar|Amritsar]] and other towns, as well as across the border in Pakistani Punjab, still embroider it. Most modern pieces use cheaper threads and lighter cloth, and many patterns are printed onto the fabric first to speed things up.

In 2011, phulkari from parts of Punjab, Haryana and Rajasthan received a GI tag, a label that protects crafts linked to a particular region. You will now see phulkari on dupattas, jackets, bags and shoes, and on bright costumes in [[@bhangra|bhangra]] performances, where it flashes as the dancers spin.

text: A scientist is someone whose job is to find out how the world works, and to prove it. They ask a question, make a careful guess called a [[hypothesis|hypothesis]], then design a test that could show the guess is wrong. They measure, record, repeat and share what they find, so others can check it.

Some scientists work in labs with test tubes and [[@microscopes|microscopes]]. Others count tigers in forests, drill into ice in Antarctica, study stars through telescopes or write computer programs that model the weather. What they share is a way of thinking: trust evidence, not just opinion, including your own.

sec.t:
There is no single scientist's day, but many weeks look like this. Some time goes into experiments or fieldwork. A lot goes into reading what other scientists have found, so you do not repeat their work. There is data to clean up and analyse, often on a computer, because measurements are rarely tidy.

Then there is writing. Scientists write papers describing what they did, applications asking for money to fund the next project, and reports for the government or companies that paid for the research. Many also teach students. Meetings and emails take up a surprising amount of time, just as in most jobs.

sec.h: The blue sea of C. V. Raman

sec.t:
Science works because scientists do not trust results until they have been checked. Before a paper is published in a journal, it is sent to other experts in the same field. This is called peer review. Reviewers point out mistakes, ask for more tests or reject the work.

Even after publication, others try to repeat the experiment. If they cannot, the original claim is doubted. Scientists are also trained to watch for traps, like a medicine that seems to work only because patients expect it to, which is known as the [[@placebo|placebo]] effect.

In 1960, a young Englishwoman named Jane Goodall began watching wild chimpanzees in Gombe, Tanzania. For months they ran away from her. Slowly they got used to her presence. Then she saw a chimp strip leaves from a twig and use it to fish termites out of a mound. Until then, many people thought only humans made tools. Her work lasted more than 60 years and changed how we see animals. It began with patience, a notebook and careful watching.

Most scientists study for many years, often finishing a PhD, a degree based on doing original research. In India, many train at universities and institutes such as IISc in Bengaluru or the IITs. In the USA, research happens at universities and agencies like NASA and the National Institutes of Health.

But the habits start young. Asking why, measuring carefully, writing things down and admitting when you were wrong are the daily tools of the job. [[@jagadish-bose|Jagadish Chandra Bose]], who studied radio waves and plants a century ago, once built his own instruments because the right ones did not exist. Plenty of scientists still do.

text: Kailash Satyarthi is an Indian campaigner who has spent more than 40 years fighting [[@child-labour|child labour]], which means children being made to work instead of going to school. In 1980 he founded Bachpan Bachao Andolan, the "Save the Childhood Movement".

His teams have raided factories, brick [[kiln|kilns]] and workshops where children were kept working, often with police, and brought the children out. His organisation says it has freed more than a lakh children.
In 2014, he shared the [[@nobel-peace|Nobel Peace Prize]] with Malala Yousafzai. The prize honoured both for their struggle for every child's right to education.

The ILO and UNICEF estimated that about 16 crore (160 million) children were in child labour in 2020, roughly 1 in 10 children worldwide. It happens in poorer and richer countries alike, on farms, in workshops and in homes.

sec.h: A boy at the school gate
sec.t:
Satyarthi was born in 1954 in Vidisha, a town in [[@madhya-pradesh|Madhya Pradesh]]. He has often told a story from his first day of school. Outside the gate sat a boy his own age, polishing shoes with his father.

Young Kailash asked his teacher why that boy wasn't in class. The answer was that poor children often had to work. The question stayed with him.

He grew up, trained as an electrical engineer and began teaching. Then, at 26, he gave it up to work against child labour full time.

In 1998, Satyarthi helped organise the Global March Against Child Labour. Children and adults marched, rode and flew about 80,000 km through more than 100 countries, ending in Geneva, Switzerland.

The next year, the International Labour Organization agreed a new [[treaty|treaty]] against the worst kinds of child labour. Many people credit the march with helping to push it through.

He also helped start a label, now called GoodWeave, that certifies carpets made without children. India's long tradition of [[@textiles-india|weaving and textiles]] is world famous, and the label lets buyers choose rugs made fairly.

Freeing children angers people who profit from their work. Satyarthi and his colleagues have been threatened and attacked during rescue raids, and two of his co-workers were killed over the years. He has said he never thought of stopping.

He also argued that the problem was bigger than a few cruel factory owners. Poverty pushes families to send children to work. Buyers want cheap goods. Schools are sometimes too far away or too poor. So his work moved beyond raids to campaigning for laws, better schools and fair shopping.

When he won the Nobel Prize in 2014, many Indians had never heard his name. Overnight, child labour was front-page news across the country.

India has made strong laws over the years. The Right to Education Act of 2009 promises free schooling to every child aged 6 to 14, and a 2016 law bans employing children under 14 in almost all work.

Child labour has fallen worldwide since 2000, but millions of children still work. Satyarthi often says a child freed is a child who gets to be a child again.

text: Estimating means finding a number that is close enough to be useful, when counting exactly would be too slow or impossible.

The trick is not to guess the whole answer at once. Break the big question into smaller ones that you can guess sensibly. How many classrooms are in your school? How many children in each? Multiply, and you have a decent estimate of the whole school.

Round your numbers to make the sums easy. Thirty-two children per class becomes 30. Eleven classes becomes 10. You aren't aiming to be exact. You want to be in the right range, not wrong by ten times.

A good estimate is careful reasoning with round numbers. You break the problem into parts you can sensibly guess, then multiply them together. Errors in different parts often cancel out, so the final answer can be surprisingly close.
facts: a big estimate built from small guesses

sec.t:
The Italian-American physicist Enrico Fermi, who won the Nobel Prize in 1938, loved this kind of question. He would ask his students things like "How many piano tuners are there in [[@chicago|Chicago]]?"

Nobody knows that number offhand. But you can reason it out. Guess how many people live in Chicago, how many homes have pianos, how often a piano needs tuning and how many pianos one tuner can manage in a year. Multiply and divide, and you get an answer that is often surprisingly close.

Questions like this are now called Fermi problems. Scientists, engineers and business people use them to check whether an idea is even possible before spending time on it.

Here is a Fermi problem you can [[@mental-maths|do in your head]]. How many times will your heart beat in your life?

A resting heart beats about 70 times a minute. Round it to 70. There are 60 minutes in an hour, so that's about 4,000 beats an hour. There are 24 hours in a day, so about 1 lakh (100,000) beats a day. A year has about 365 days, so roughly 3.5 crore beats a year.

If you live 80 years, that's about 300 crore, or 3 billion, [[@heart-beat|heartbeats]]. The real number depends on your heart and how active you are, but the estimate is in the right ballpark.

{{story:heart-beat}}

In 1906, the English scientist Francis Galton visited a farm fair in Plymouth. Visitors paid a small fee to guess the weight of an ox, with prizes for the closest. Galton collected about 800 tickets.

Some guessers were butchers and farmers. Most were ordinary visitors who knew little about cattle. Galton expected the crowd to be poor at it. Instead, when he lined up all the guesses, the middle one was 1,207 pounds. The ox weighed 1,198 pounds. The crowd's [[@averages|median]] guess was off by less than 1%.

The lesson is that many independent guesses, each wrong in different ways, can average out to something close to the truth. It works best when people guess on their own without copying each other.

Police and event organisers estimate crowds at festivals and marches. They work out the area of a space, then guess how many people fit into each square metre. Loosely packed crowds might have one or two people per square metre. Very tightly packed ones can reach four or more.

Governments sometimes estimate [[@population|population]] between [[census|censuses]] using birth and death records. A full [[@census|census]] is the careful count that checks those estimates.

Estimating is also a way of catching mistakes. If you work out a shopping bill and get ₹4,500 for a few vegetables, a quick estimate tells you something has gone wrong. Engineers do the same with [[@bridges|bridges]] and buildings. If the calculator and the rough guess disagree by ten times, it's time to check again.

myth: Dhoni never felt nervous during big matches.
Dhoni has said he did feel pressure, but focused on the process of each ball rather than the result. Staying calm on the outside was a skill he worked on.

sec.t:
Dhoni was born in Ranchi in 1981. The city was then in Bihar and is now in Jharkhand. Few big cricketers had come from there. At school he played badminton and was the goalkeeper of the football team. When the cricket team needed a wicketkeeper, he was asked to try.

He was good, but it took years to break through. From about 2001 to 2003 he worked as a travelling ticket examiner for [[@indian-railways|Indian Railways]] at Kharagpur station in West Bengal. He played cricket for the railway team and kept practising.

sec.h: The long hair and the big hits

sec.t:
In 2007 a young Indian team with Dhoni as captain won the first T20 World Cup in South Africa. In the final against Pakistan he gave the last over to Joginder Sharma, a surprising choice that worked.

On 2 April 2011, at the Wankhede Stadium in Mumbai, India needed four runs to win the World Cup final against Sri Lanka. Dhoni hit Nuwan Kulasekara for six. He had promoted himself up the batting order that night and scored 91 not out. In 2013 India also won the Champions Trophy in England. In between, in 2009, he led India to the top of the Test rankings for the first time. Many of the young players he backed, like Rohit Sharma and Virat Kohli, went on to become captains themselves.

Dhoni rarely shouted at players or argued with umpires. He has said he tried to focus on the next ball, not the final score. Teammates said this helped young players feel safe under [[@stress|pressure]].

He also made bold decisions quietly. He retired from [[@test-cricket|Test cricket]] halfway through a series in Australia in 2014, and announced his international retirement on Instagram on 15 August 2020, India's Independence Day.

In the IPL, Dhoni has captained Chennai Super Kings to five titles. Fans in [[@chennai|Chennai]] call him "Thala", a Tamil word meaning head or leader. Yellow-shirted crowds fill stadiums across India just to watch him walk out to bat.

The Indian Army made him an honorary Lieutenant Colonel in the Territorial Army in 2011. He loves motorbikes, and keeps a large collection at his home in Ranchi, the city that now has a cricket stadium where he once dreamed of playing.

text: A growth spurt is a stretch of time when your body grows much faster than usual. The biggest one happens at puberty, the years when a child's body changes into an adult's. During it, many teenagers grow 8 to 10 cm in a single year.

Girls usually start their spurt earlier, often around 10 or 11. Boys usually start a couple of years later, around 12 or 13, and keep going longer. That's why, in many classrooms, girls are taller than boys for a few years, before the boys catch up.
Smaller spurts happen in early childhood too. And the very fastest growth of your life was when you were a baby.

options.t: Your first year as a baby
Your teenage growth spurt
Between ages 5 and 8

st.reveal: A typical baby grows about 25 cm in the first year, half as long again as at birth. The teenage spurt is fast, but at about 8 to 10 cm a year at its peak, it does not beat babyhood.

d.try: Ask an adult to mark your height on a strip of paper taped to a door, with the date, once every three months. After a year, plot the marks on a simple line graph. You might spot that you grow faster in some seasons than others, which many children do.
myth: Drinking tea or coffee will stunt your growth.

There is no good evidence that tea or coffee make children shorter. Height depends mostly on genes, good food and enough sleep. Doctors still suggest kids keep caffeine low, because it can disturb sleep.

sec.t:
A newborn is usually about 50 cm long. By its first birthday, it is often about 75 cm. That is 25 cm in one year, half its own length again. If you kept growing at that rate, by age 13 you would be taller than an Indian elephant.

After that first year, growth slows down to about 5 to 7 cm a year through childhood. Then puberty arrives and the speed jumps again, for two or three years, before slowing to a stop.

Puberty begins in the brain. A small [[gland|gland]] under the brain, the pituitary, starts sending out signals called [[@hormones|hormones]]. They tell the body to make more growth [[hormone|hormone]] and sex hormones such as oestrogen and testosterone.

Those hormones act on the [[@bones-growth|growth plates]], soft layers of [[cartilage|cartilage]] near the ends of long bones like the thigh and shin. Cells there multiply and turn into new bone, making the bone longer. At the end of puberty, the hormones also tell the growth plates to harden and close. Once that happens, you cannot grow taller.

Much growth hormone is released in deep sleep at night. That is one more good reason to get enough [[@sleep-why|sleep]].

sec.h: Big feet, long legs, awkward elbows
sec.t:
The body does not grow evenly. Hands and feet usually go first, then arms and legs, and the chest and back last. So a 12-year-old might suddenly need much bigger shoes long before the rest of the body catches up.

Because legs and arms lengthen fast, the brain has to keep updating its map of where they are. For a while, it can feel like you are always banging your knee or tripping on the stairs. It passes.

Many children also feel hungrier than ever during a spurt. Their bodies need extra energy and building blocks such as [[protein|protein]] and calcium. Some feel tired, or get achy legs at night, often called growing pains, though doctors are not sure growth itself causes them.

Two children of the same age can be at very different stages. One might finish growing at 13 while a friend has not started. Both can be perfectly normal. Your final height mostly depends on the [[gene|genes]] from your parents, plus good food, sleep and health along the way.

Average heights have changed over time too. In many countries, people today are taller than their great-grandparents, mainly because of better food and less disease. Indian children have been getting taller on average over the past century, though more slowly than in some other countries.

Doctors track a child's growth by plotting height on a chart over the years, which turns a set of marks on a door frame into a [[@graphs-charts|graph]] with a story. If you ever worry that you are growing too fast or too slowly, a doctor can look at that chart and tell you what is normal for you.

Still, no human comes close to the champions of growth. Some kinds of [[@bamboo|bamboo]] can grow almost a metre in a single day, fast enough that you could nearly watch it happen.

text: When you start to run, your [[@muscles|muscles]] need much more energy. They make it by burning sugar and fat, and for that they need oxygen. So your whole body works to deliver more.

Your heart beats faster and harder, pumping more blood. You breathe faster and deeper to pull in oxygen and push out [[carbon-dioxide|carbon dioxide]]. Blood vessels in your muscles open wider, while those in your stomach narrow a little. All that burning makes heat, so you get hot and start to [[@sweat|sweat]]. Your brain releases chemicals that can lift your mood. Do this often, and your body adapts: your heart, lungs, muscles and bones all get stronger.

st.prompt: You're sprinting as hard as you can. Why do your legs start burning after about half a minute?

The muscles are running out of water

st.reveal: When you sprint, your muscles burn fuel faster than oxygen can arrive. They switch to a quick backup way of making energy, which leaves acidic by-products behind. The burning fades within minutes once you slow down.

myth: Lactic acid causes the sore muscles you feel the day after exercise.

The burning chemicals made during hard exercise are cleared within about an hour. The stiffness that comes a day or two later is caused by tiny tears and swelling in muscle fibres as they repair and get stronger.

sec.t:
In the first few seconds of a sprint, muscles use a small store of ready energy that lasts only moments. Then they start breaking down sugar stored inside them. Your [[@heartbeat-exercise|heart rate]] climbs from around 80 beats a minute to well over 150.

Your [[@lungs-breathe|lungs]] can move more than ten times as much air during hard exercise as at rest. If you're [[@body-speed-limit|running as fast as you can]], the muscles still can't get oxygen quickly enough. They switch to a faster backup method that leaves acidic leftovers. That's the burning feeling in your legs, and the reason you can't sprint flat out for long.

Hard exercise causes tiny tears in muscle fibres. You don't feel them at first. A day or two later, your muscles may feel stiff and sore as your body repairs them. Each repair makes them a little stronger.

[[@bones|Bones]] get stronger too. When you jump, run and climb, the pull and push on your bones tell them to add more mineral. Children who are active build stronger bones that last into old age. Rest matters as much as exercise, since that's when the rebuilding happens, mostly during [[@sleep-why|sleep]].

sec.h: Good for the brain as well
sec.t:
Exercise sends more blood to the [[@brain-works|brain]]. Many studies have found that active children tend to concentrate better and sleep more soundly. Exercise also releases chemicals that can make you feel calmer and happier.

The World Health Organization suggests children and teenagers get about an hour of activity a day, mostly the kind that makes you breathe hard. It doesn't need to be a sport. A game of [[@kho-kho|kho-kho]] in the school yard, a long bike ride, dancing at a wedding, [[@life-games-playground|a game of tag]] or a [[@basketball|basketball]] game in a park all count. So does walking to school.

Sitting still for hours has the opposite effect. Muscles get weaker and the heart gets less practice. Health experts suggest breaking up long stretches of sitting, even just by standing up and moving around for a few minutes every hour.

text: Throwing up is an emergency exit. When your body thinks there's something harmful in your stomach, like germs, spoiled food or a poison, it pushes it back out. Better out the way it came in than left to do more damage.

The order comes from your brain, not your stomach. A control area in the brainstem listens for warning signals. Some come from nerves in the gut, some from chemicals in the blood, and some from the balance organs in your inner ear. When enough warnings pile up, the brain starts a fixed routine, a bit like a fire drill.

st.prompt: Which part of your body decides that it is time to throw up?

options.t: The brain
The stomach
The throat

st.reveal: A control area in the brainstem collects alarm signals from the stomach, the inner ear and the blood. When enough alarms go off, it runs the whole sequence of squeezing muscles. The stomach itself is fairly passive.

d.try: Sit on a spinning chair with your eyes closed while a friend turns you slowly a few times, then stop and open your eyes. Notice how the room seems to keep moving. That mismatch between your eyes and your inner ear is what causes motion sickness. Stop straight away if you feel queasy.
myth: Throwing up always means something is seriously wrong.

Most vomiting is the body getting rid of something it doesn't like, such as a stomach bug or spoiled food, and it passes in a day or so. It is worth telling a trusted adult or doctor if it goes on, if there is blood, or if someone can't keep water down.

sec.t:
First you feel sick, the feeling doctors call nausea. Your mouth fills with extra [[saliva|saliva]], which helps protect your teeth from the [[acid|acid]] about to come up. You might go pale and sweaty.

Next, you take a deep breath and a flap closes over your windpipe so nothing goes into your lungs. Then the [[diaphragm|diaphragm]], the big dome-shaped muscle under your lungs, and your belly muscles squeeze hard together, all at once. The stomach is pressed like a tube of toothpaste. A ring of muscle at its top relaxes, and out it all comes.

The stomach doesn't do most of the pushing. It is more like a balloon being squashed by the muscles around it.

sec.h: Why cars and boats do it
sec.t:
Germs are not the only trigger. On a winding road or a rocking boat, your eyes may see a still car or cabin while your inner ear feels movement. Your brain gets two stories that don't match.

One old idea is that the brain treats this mismatch as a sign of poisoning, because some poisons make you dizzy. So it plays safe and empties the stomach. Scientists still debate whether that's the full reason, but it explains why [[@motion-sickness|motion sickness]] feels so much like food poisoning.

In space, the mismatch is even stronger. With no "up" or "down", roughly half of astronauts feel sick in their first days. NASA trains astronauts in a plane that dives to make short bursts of weightlessness. It earned the nickname "Vomit Comet".

{{story:space-body}}

sec.h: Animals that throw up on purpose
sec.t:
Humans aren't the only ones. Dogs and cats throw up often, sometimes after eating grass. Owls swallow mice whole and later cough up neat pellets of fur and bone.

Some animals use vomit as a weapon. Vultures can throw up foul-smelling food when threatened, which makes them lighter for take-off and puts attackers off. [[@vultures-india|India's vultures]] belong to this group.

Rats and horses, oddly, can't throw up at all. Their bodies aren't built for it, which is one reason rat poison works and why horses must be fed carefully.

Most people feel a bit better after vomiting, because the source of trouble has gone. The biggest danger afterwards is losing too much water and salt, especially for small children. Sips of water or an oral rehydration drink help. Rest helps too.

Vomiting is the body's version of an alarm that goes off a little too easily. Better a false alarm than a real poison staying inside. And the strangest version of this trick belongs to a beetle that toads swallow and then throw up alive, thanks to the boiling spray of the [[@power-bombardier-beetle|bombardier beetle]].

text: The Renaissance was a time of great change in European art, science and ideas, from about 1350 to 1600. It began in Italy, especially in the city of Florence, and spread across Europe.

The word means "rebirth". Renaissance scholars believed they were bringing back the learning of [[@ancient-greece|ancient Greece]] and Rome. They studied old texts, asked questions about the world and celebrated what humans could achieve, an outlook called humanism. Artists such as [[@leonardo|Leonardo]] da Vinci and [[@michelangelo|Michelangelo]] made paintings and [[sculpture|sculptures]] that looked startlingly real. Architects designed buildings inspired by Roman ruins, and the [[@printing-press|printing press]] let new ideas spread faster than ever before.

st.reveal: Brunelleschi built two domes, an inner and an outer, joined together. Bricks set in a zigzag herringbone pattern locked each new ring in place as it rose. He also designed new hoisting machines to lift the materials.

myth: The Middle Ages were a "dark age" when nobody in Europe learned anything.
Medieval Europe had universities, great cathedrals and scholars, and learning thrived in the Islamic world, India and China at the same time. Renaissance thinkers built on all of this.

sec.t:
In the 1400s, Florence was rich from banking and the wool and cloth trade. Wealthy families, especially the Medici, competed to show off their money and taste. They paid artists, architects and scholars to work for them. Someone who funds artists in this way is called a patron.

Florence was also a [[republic|republic]] of proud citizens and busy workshops. Young artists trained as apprentices, grinding colours and copying their masters before taking on work of their own. Talent, money and rivalry came together in one small city.

sec.h: A dome and a vanishing point

sec.t:
The Renaissance did not come only from Europe's own past. Many ancient Greek books had been preserved and studied in Arabic by scholars in Baghdad, [[@world-cairo|Cairo]] and Spain. Their own work in medicine, astronomy and mathematics was translated into Latin.

[[@indian-numerals|Indian numerals]], including zero, travelled the same way. In 1202 the Italian mathematician [[@maths-golden-spiral|Fibonacci]] wrote a book explaining these "Hindu-Arabic" [[@number-systems|numbers]] to European merchants. They were far easier to use than [[@roman-numerals|Roman numerals]]. When Constantinople fell to the [[@ottomans|Ottomans]] in 1453, Greek scholars fled to Italy, bringing more texts.

Leonardo da Vinci painted the *[[@famous-paintings|Mona Lisa]]* and filled notebooks with drawings of machines, birds and the human body. Michelangelo carved his marble *David*, over 5 metres tall, and spent four years painting the ceiling of the [[@vatican|Sistine Chapel]] in Rome, from 1508 to 1512.

Scientists began to test old ideas with observation. In 1543 Nicolaus Copernicus argued that the Earth goes around the Sun. Later, [[@galileo|Galileo]] pointed a telescope at the sky and found moons orbiting [[@jupiter-giant|Jupiter]].

People at the time did talk about a revival of learning. But the word "Renaissance" for the whole era became popular only in the 19th century, especially after the Swiss historian Jacob Burckhardt wrote about it in 1860.

Today many historians are cautious about the label. Change came slowly, and mostly reached the rich and educated. Ordinary farmers' lives changed little. Still, the art of this age, from the dome of Florence to the *Mona Lisa*, draws millions of visitors every year.

text: Srivijaya was a sea-trading kingdom based on the island of Sumatra, in today's Indonesia. From about the 7th century to the 13th century, it controlled the narrow waters between Sumatra and the Malay Peninsula. Almost every ship sailing between India and China had to pass that way.

Srivijaya didn't need huge armies on land. It used a strong fleet to keep pirates away, made ships stop at its ports and charged them for the privilege. In return, traders got safe harbours, fresh water, and a market where Chinese silk, Indian cloth and island spices changed hands.
It was also a great centre of Buddhism, where monks from China stopped to study on their way to India.

st.prompt: Srivijaya grew rich without large farmlands or famous mines. What was its main source of wealth?

options.t: Controlling a narrow sea passage that trading ships had to use
Selling diamonds dug from its mountains
Taxing farmers who grew wheat

st.reveal: Ships sailing between India and China had to pass through the Strait of Malacca or the Sunda Strait. Srivijaya made sure they stopped at its ports, paid fees and traded there.

n.certNote: Srivijaya left few buildings, so historians piece it together from stone inscriptions, Chinese and Arab records and finds from the seabed. Experts still debate exactly where its capital was at different times and how much land it really ruled.

Apart from raids like the Chola one, Southeast Asian kingdoms such as Srivijaya were ruled by local kings. They chose to adopt ideas from India, including Buddhism, Sanskrit words and styles of art, through trade and learning.

sec.t:
Look at a map and you'll see why it worked. Ships from the Bay of Bengal heading for China had to squeeze through the Strait of Malacca, or the Sunda Strait further south. Both were within Srivijaya's reach.

Sailors also had to wait for the [[@monsoon|monsoon]] winds to change before going on. That meant weeks or months in port, buying food, repairing ships and trading. Srivijaya's harbours, probably near today's city of Palembang, filled with boats from Arabia, India and China. Srivijaya also sold goods from Sumatra's own forests and hills, such as camphor, sweet-smelling resins and gold. Rivers carried them down to the coast.

The earliest stone [[inscription|inscription]] that names Srivijaya, found near Palembang, dates to 682 CE. It is written in Old Malay using an Indian-style script, and it tells of a king leading thousands of soldiers on a holy journey.

In 671, a Chinese monk named Yijing stopped in Srivijaya on his way to India. He found more than a thousand Buddhist monks there, and he advised other Chinese pilgrims to study Sanskrit in Srivijaya before going on to India.

Yijing later spent years at [[@nalanda|Nalanda]], the great Buddhist university in Bihar. Then he returned to Srivijaya and stayed for years more, copying and translating texts.

The link with Nalanda was close. In the 9th century, a king named Balaputradeva, from the Sailendra family that ruled Srivijaya, paid for a [[monastery|monastery]] at Nalanda. A copper plate issued by Devapala, a king of Bengal, records the gift.

{{story:monsoon}}

Wealth brought enemies. Around 1025, the Tamil king Rajendra I sent [[@chola-navy|the Chola navy]] across the Bay of Bengal. His inscriptions list a string of Srivijayan ports that his forces attacked, and say he captured the king.

Historians still argue about why. Some think the Cholas wanted to protect their own merchants' trade with China. The raid didn't destroy Srivijaya, but it left the kingdom weaker.

Over the next centuries, rival ports grew, Javanese kingdoms became stronger, and Chinese merchants began sailing direct to more ports. By the late 13th century, Srivijaya had faded.

Because its buildings were mostly made of wood, little was left to see. The name nearly vanished. In 1918, the French scholar George Cœdès matched Chinese records of a kingdom called "Shilifoshi" with old Sumatran inscriptions and showed they were the same place.

Srivijaya's story lives on in the monuments of its neighbours and relatives. The Sailendra rulers in Java built [[@borobudur|Borobudur]], the largest Buddhist monument in the world, around the 8th and 9th centuries. Divers have found wrecks of trading ships in Indonesian waters full of Chinese pottery, the same kind of cargo that once passed through Srivijaya's ports. The Malay language, now spoken by millions, grew in part from the Old Malay of its inscriptions.

text: Mount Rushmore was carved to bring visitors to South Dakota and to celebrate the story of the United States. In 1923, a historian named Doane Robinson suggested carving giant figures in the Black Hills to attract tourists. The sculptor Gutzon Borglum took on the job and chose [[@usa-presidents-facts|four presidents]].

The National Park Service explains the choice like this. [[@george-washington|George Washington]] stands for the birth of the nation and [[@thomas-jefferson|Thomas Jefferson]] for its growth. [[@pop-teddy-bear|Theodore Roosevelt]] stands for its development, and [[@abraham-lincoln|Abraham Lincoln]] for holding it together through the [[@us-civil-war|Civil War]]. Work began in 1927 and stopped in 1941. Today more than two million people visit each year.

With hammers and chisels
With water jets

st.reveal: About 90% of the rock, roughly 400,000 tonnes, was removed by blasting. Workers then used drills and hammers to shape the details, finishing the surface until it was as smooth as a pavement.

d.try: Carve your own head. Take a bar of soap and draw a simple face on one side with a pencil. With a blunt lolly stick or plastic spoon, scrape away the soap around the nose first, since it sticks out furthest. Then work on the eyes and mouth. Borglum used the same idea, starting from a model and the highest points.

sec.t:
Each face is about 18 m tall, roughly the height of a six-storey building. Washington's nose is about 6 m long, about as long as two autorickshaws parked nose to tail. The eyes have a block of rock left in the middle of each pupil, which catches sunlight and makes them seem to sparkle from far away.

The original plan was to carve the presidents down to their waists. Money ran short, and Borglum died in March 1941. His son Lincoln Borglum finished the faces, and work stopped in October that year. The [[@rocks-types|granite]] is so hard that it wears away by only about 2.5 cm every 10,000 years.

Borglum planned a great Hall of Records inside the mountain behind Lincoln's head, to store America's most important documents for future people to find. Workers cut a tunnel about 21 m deep before the project stopped. In 1998, a vault was placed in the floor of the tunnel, holding panels with the text of key documents and the story of the carving.

The Black Hills, called Paha Sapa in Lakota, are sacred to the Lakota people and other Native nations. In the Treaty of Fort Laramie of 1868, the US government promised the Black Hills to the Lakota. After gold was found there in 1874, settlers and miners poured in, and the government took the land.

In 1980, the US Supreme Court ruled that the land had been taken illegally and ordered the government to pay. The Lakota refused the money, saying they want the land back instead. The money has grown in a fund to well over a billion dollars and has never been collected. For many Lakota, Mount Rushmore is a painful reminder of that history.

About 27 km away, another giant carving has been under way since 1948. The Crazy Horse Memorial honours a Lakota leader. Its face, about 27 m tall, was finished in 1998, but the whole [[sculpture|sculpture]], showing him on horseback, may take many more decades. Like India's [[@statue-of-unity|Statue of Unity]], these giant [[@national-symbols|national symbols]] show how nations use huge carvings to tell their stories, and how people can see the same story differently.

text: *The Jungle Book* is a collection of stories by Rudyard Kipling, published in 1894. The most famous ones are about Mowgli, a boy raised by [[@wolves-india|wolves]] in the forests of central India. He is taught the Law of the Jungle by Baloo the bear and Bagheera the black panther, and hunted by Shere Khan, the tiger.

Kipling was born in Bombay in 1865, but he wrote the book thousands of kilometres away. He was living in the US state of Vermont with his American wife. A second collection, *The Second Jungle Book*, followed in 1895. Together they have been retold in films, cartoons and plays ever since.

sec.t:
The Mowgli stories are set in the Seoni hills, in what is now [[@madhya-pradesh|Madhya Pradesh]]. Kipling probably never visited Seoni himself, but he read reports by British forest officers and drew on what he remembered of India.

In the stories, the jungle is not wild chaos. It has a Law. The wolf pack meets at Council Rock, led by the old wolf Akela. Animals must not kill humans, and they must share water during a [[drought|drought]]. Shere Khan breaks the Law, which is why the others look down on him. The monkeys, the Bandar-log, are mocked for having no law at all.

Many names come from Hindi. Baloo is from *bhalu* (bear), Hathi means elephant, and Shere Khan combines *sher* (tiger) with a title, Khan. Mowgli, though, is Kipling's own invention.

{{story:tiger-stripes}}

Only some of the stories are about Mowgli. "Rikki-Tikki-Tavi" tells of a brave mongoose who protects an English family's garden from two cobras, Nag and Nagaina. "Toomai of the Elephants" follows a boy who sees elephants dance in the forest at night. "The White Seal" is set far away in the icy Bering Sea.

Each story ends with a poem or song. Kipling cared about [[rhythm|rhythm]] and the sound of words, which is one reason his sentences are fun to read aloud.

The book quickly travelled beyond readers. In 1916, the founder of the Scout movement, Robert Baden-Powell, used it to shape his new programme for younger boys, the Wolf Cubs. Cub groups are still called packs, and the adult leader is still called Akela in many countries, part of [[@scouts-guides|Scouting]] today.

Disney's animated film of 1967 made the story famous worldwide, with Baloo singing "The Bare Necessities". It changed the story a lot, making it lighter and funnier. In 2016, Disney made a live-action version, with an Indian-American boy, Neel Sethi, as Mowgli and computer-made animals.

For many Indian children, the best-known version is a Japanese animated series that was dubbed into Hindi and shown on Doordarshan in the early 1990s. Its theme song, with lyrics by the poet Gulzar, began "Jungle jungle baat chali hai, pata chala hai", and millions of children could sing it. It became one of the most loved shows of the time on [[@tv-india|Indian television]].

Readers today sometimes feel uneasy about Kipling, who supported the British Empire. Some see the jungle's strict Law and hierarchy as an echo of his ideas about rule and order. Even so, the forests he described, with their wolves, langurs and tigers, are real, and several [[@national-parks|national parks]] in central India still protect them. Pench Tiger Reserve, close to Seoni, is often described as the real Jungle Book country, and visitors there can still hear langurs bark their warning when a tiger is near.
